title: Why Is Marriage Under Spiritual Attack?
paragraphs:
Why Is Marriage Under Spiritual Attack?
Because the Enemy Does Not Need to Destroy Your Wedding Day if He Can Slowly Convince You to Destroy Each Other
There is a kind of silence that only married people understand.
Two people can sleep inches apart and feel miles away.
The house can look normal.
The children can be fed.
The bills can be paid.
The wedding photos can still hang beautifully on the wall.
You can still say “we’re fine” when someone asks.
And yet something inside the marriage is bleeding.
Not always because someone committed adultery.
Not always because someone packed a suitcase.
Sometimes marriages begin dying in smaller rooms.
A conversation that keeps getting postponed.
An apology nobody wants to make.
A phone turned face-down.
A husband who stopped feeling respected.
A wife who stopped feeling cherished.
A wound that became resentment.
Resentment that became distance.
Distance that became secrecy.
Secrecy that eventually began feeling more comfortable than intimacy.
And somewhere in that slow unraveling, two people who once promised, “I will never leave you,” begin quietly wondering how they became strangers.
This is where we must be careful.
Because when Christians say marriage is “under spiritual attack,” we can become so dramatic that we stop being biblical.
Not every disagreement is a demon.
Not every difficult season is Satan.
Not every marriage problem can be solved merely by rebuking the devil.
Sometimes the problem is pride.
Sometimes it is selfishness.
Sometimes it is pornography.
Sometimes it is uncontrolled anger.
Sometimes it is financial dishonesty.
Sometimes it is emotional neglect.
Sometimes it is adultery.
Sometimes it is refusing to forgive.
Sometimes it is refusing to repent.
Sometimes it is years of wounds that were covered with Christian language instead of actually confronted.
And sometimes what someone calls “spiritual warfare” is really the painful harvest of choices Scripture already warned us not to make.
But none of that means spiritual warfare is imaginary.
Scripture gives us a far more sober picture.
“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood…” Paul writes in Ephesians 6:12.
That changes the atmosphere of the argument.
Because suddenly the person sitting across from you is not automatically the enemy.
Your spouse is not Satan.
Your husband is not the devil.
Your wife is not the devil.
And if the enemy can persuade you to treat the person God called you to love as though that person were the ultimate enemy, he has already gained ground.
Read that again.
The person you are fighting may not be the real enemy.
And the real enemy may be delighted that you have forgotten that.
Marriage matters spiritually because marriage was not invented by Hollywood, governments, wedding planners, or modern culture. Its biblical roots reach all the way back to creation.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew ending is striking:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
Not merely two roommates sharing expenses.
Not merely two people enjoying romantic compatibility until somebody more exciting appears.
One flesh.
That does not mean husband and wife cease to be distinct persons. It means Scripture describes marriage as a profound covenantal union rather than a disposable arrangement.
Then Jesus reaches back to this creation text in Matthew 19 and says:
ὃ οὖν ὁ Θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.
ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō.
“What therefore God has joined together, let man not separate.”

The word συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen carries the idea of joining or yoking together. Jesus is not describing marriage as something casually assembled and casually discarded. He points beyond the ceremony to God Himself as the One who joins.
Now perhaps you understand why marriage becomes a battlefield.
Marriage asks two sinners to practice something our fallen nature hates:
dying to self.
Marriage exposes you.
It eventually discovers the version of you that dating never met.
The impatient you.
The exhausted you.
The insecure you.
The selfish you.
The sexually tempted you.
The financially frightened you.
The defensive you.
The wounded you.
The you who wants grace when you fail but justice when your spouse fails.
Marriage has an uncomfortable way of revealing how much of Christianity we actually believe when another human being inconveniences us.
It is easy to preach grace.
It is harder to give grace at 11:47 at night when you are angry.
It is easy to quote “love is patient.”
It is harder to be patient when the same argument has happened twenty times.
It is easy to sing about surrender on Sunday.
It is harder to surrender your pride on Tuesday.
And that is one reason the enemy loves division.
Because biblical marriage continually confronts the kingdom of self.
But there is something even deeper.
Paul speaks of marriage in Ephesians 5 and then says something astonishing:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Marriage does not replace the Gospel.
Marriage does not save anyone.
A spouse cannot do what only Jesus can do.
But Christian marriage is called to display something beyond itself—the covenant love of Christ and His people.
That is why a husband is not simply commanded to “provide.”
He is commanded:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Think about the weight of that.
Not “love her when she makes you happy.”
Not “love her until she ages.”
Not “love her until marriage becomes inconvenient.”
Christ loved sacrificially.
Christ gave Himself.
Christian husband, your masculinity is not proven by how effectively you can dominate your household.
Look at Jesus.
Strength kneels.
Strength serves.
Strength sacrifices.
Strength tells the truth.
Strength remains sexually faithful.
Strength repents when wrong.
Strength protects without becoming controlling.
Strength does not use Scripture as a weapon to terrify the woman it was commanded to love.
And wife, biblical submission is never permission for sin, coercion, violence, degradation, or abuse. Scripture never turns another human being into someone’s private god. Christ remains Lord.
This matters because some people reading this article are not merely experiencing “marriage difficulties.”
Some are frightened.
Some are being threatened.
Some have been physically harmed.
Some have been sexually coerced.
Some are living beneath manipulation dressed in religious vocabulary.
Do not allow anyone to weaponize “God hates divorce,” “wives submit,” or “forgive seventy times seven” to demand that a victim silently remain in immediate danger.
Seeking safety, wise pastoral care, appropriate professional help, and lawful protection when necessary is not the same thing as refusing to honor marriage.
Biblical covenant faithfulness never requires pretending evil is good.
And repentance is not merely saying, “Sorry.”
Repentance produces a changed direction.
That distinction matters.
Because the enemy attacks marriage not only through obvious destruction, but through counterfeit spirituality.
He would be perfectly content for a husband to know Greek words while refusing to apologize.
He would be perfectly content for a wife to post Bible verses while secretly feeding an emotional affair.
He does not care how loudly you worship if you continually refuse to repent.
He does not tremble because your wedding was held in a church building.
What matters is whether Jesus Christ is actually Lord of what happens after the photographs are taken.
Hebrews 13:4 begins:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν
Timios ho gamos en pasin.
Marriage is to be held in honor.

The verse continues with the marriage bed being kept undefiled and warns that God judges sexual immorality and adultery. The Greek τίμιος — timios communicates something honored or precious; ἀμίαντος — amiantos means undefiled.
God takes marital faithfulness seriously.
Which means pornography is not harmless because “everybody does it.”
Flirtation is not innocent simply because nobody touched.
Secret messages do not become pure because they disappear after twenty-four hours.
An emotional affair does not become righteous because there was never a hotel room.
You know when someone is receiving emotional territory that belongs inside your covenant.
You know when you are deleting something because you do not want your spouse to see it.
You know when “we’re just friends” has started becoming something your conscience has to defend.
You know when the screen has become a secret room.
And God knows too.
This is where some readers will want to stop reading.
Please don't.
Because the Gospel is about to enter the room.
Maybe you already failed.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out your intimacy.
Maybe you became emotionally attached to someone who was not your spouse.
Maybe your temper turned your home into a place where everyone walks carefully around you.
Maybe you neglected the person you once begged God to give you.
Maybe your marriage collapsed and you know you contributed to the wreckage.
Maybe you are divorced and every article about marriage makes you feel like Christianity has already placed you in the category marked “damaged.”
Maybe your spouse abandoned you.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you fought until there was nothing left except lawyers, paperwork, memories, and the unbearable question:
“Can God still do anything with my life?”
Yes.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus does.
The Gospel does not say your sin was small.
The Gospel says Christ's cross was enough.
There is a world of difference.
At Calvary, Jesus did not pretend human rebellion was harmless. He bore sin.
He was wounded.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose.
That means Christianity offers something infinitely deeper than marriage advice.
It offers resurrection.
The scandal of grace is that Jesus receives people who finally stop defending the very things destroying them.
Adulterers can repent.
Pornography addicts can repent.
Bitter husbands can repent.
Controlling wives can repent.
Liars can repent.
The sexually broken can repent.
The proud can repent.
The emotionally unfaithful can repent.
The coldhearted can repent.
And repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is coming home.
First John 1:9 gives sinners this hope: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
That does not mean every earthly consequence instantly disappears.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust overnight.
Reconciliation cannot be manufactured by one person while another remains committed to betrayal or abuse.
A broken marriage may require pastoral counsel, qualified counseling, accountability, boundaries, disclosure, treatment, and time.
Some wounds heal slowly.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace tells the truth about what happened and then asks what Jesus can redeem from here.
That is our heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though the betrayal never occurred.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing consequences.
Jesus rewrites what gets the final word.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The affair does not have to have the final word.
The addiction does not have to have the final word.
The argument does not have to have the final word.
The separation does not have to have the final word.
Even when a marriage cannot be restored, your life is not beyond the redemptive reach of Christ.
Jesus has the final word.
And maybe the spiritual attack on marriage becomes most dangerous when we stop asking, “How do I defeat my spouse?” and finally begin asking:
“Jesus, what in me needs to die?”
Maybe you do not need another marriage quote tonight.
Maybe you need repentance.
Maybe you need to put the phone down, walk into the other room, and say:
“I was wrong.”
No excuses.
No “but you…”
No sermon.
No list of your spouse's failures.
Just truth.
“I hurt you.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I have not loved you like Christ.”
“I need forgiveness.”
“I need help.”
“I want Jesus to change me.”
There are sentences that can change the temperature of a home.
And sometimes revival does not begin behind a pulpit.
Sometimes revival begins beside a bed where two exhausted people finally stop trying to win.
Maybe you are reading this while your spouse is sleeping beside you.
Look at them.
That person is not promised to you forever on this earth.
One day, one of you may have to stand beside the other's grave.
Suddenly some of the things you are refusing to forgive look smaller.
Suddenly the conversation you keep postponing feels more urgent.
Suddenly “I'll apologize tomorrow” sounds dangerously expensive.
Love them while you can.
Pray together while you can.
Hold hands while you can.
Laugh again while you can.
Get help while you can.
Confess while you can.
Forgive what can biblically be forgiven.
Rebuild what can wisely be rebuilt.
And above everything else, seek Christ while He may be found.
Because the ultimate goal of Christian marriage is not to convince the internet that you have a perfect relationship.
You don't.
Neither does anyone else.
The goal is faithfulness to Christ.
Be honest before God first.
Someone scrolling tonight may desperately need evidence that difficult does not always mean dead.
Not because every sentence applies to every marriage, but because there may come a night when anger becomes louder than covenant and you need to remember who the actual enemy is.
Not as a badge proving that your marriage is healthy.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a way to purchase God's favor. We do not glorify God by being pressured into giving. We glorify Him through faithful obedience, generosity, truth, love, and service flowing from grace.
And there is more than merchandise behind the mission.
Send it privately to the couple nobody else knows is struggling.
And pray for us.
Because numbers are not the mission.
Souls are.
Jesus is.
Perhaps tonight the greatest spiritual victory in your marriage will not look dramatic at all.
Perhaps nobody will post about it.
Perhaps there will be no music playing in the background.
Perhaps it will simply be a husband closing a secret browser window for the last time.
A wife ending an inappropriate conversation.
Two people finally calling a counselor.
A wounded spouse choosing not revenge, but truth.
A proud heart whispering, “I was wrong.”
Two hands reaching across a cold bed.
Two sinners kneeling on the same floor.
And somewhere between tears and confession, one trembling prayer:
“Jesus… we cannot fix this without You.”
That prayer may not erase years of damage tonight.
But surrender is a beautiful place for rebuilding to begin.
Because marriage was never meant to prove that two people could become each other's savior.
Marriage needs a Savior too.
His name is Jesus.
And when the enemy whispers, “It's over,” remember this:
The cross looked like the end too—until Sunday morning.
